title: Stratified stage consolidation and NCCL fallback notes
content:
Context and goal:

This is a working note about a design that aims to reduce cross-GPU synchronization overhead and provide a robust fallback when NCCL collectives show congestion or partial failure. The focus is on: 1) opportunistically consolidating adjacent pipeline/tensor stages to reduce point-to-point communication, 2) a lightweight probe-and-degrade strategy for NCCL (bandwidth/latency-aware fallback), and 3) KV-cache sharding semantics compatible with stage consolidation and degradation.

Why this felt necessary (notes to self):
- Recent tail-latency spikes on large-context chat workloads correlate with bursty NCCL traffic (see INFR-2345).
- Standard ring all-reduce is fast when NIC/GPU pairings are healthy but collapses under partial node-level packet loss or network congestion.
- Existing shard placement assumes stable collectives; we need a mode that tolerates degraded collectives without failing requests or forcing full replication.

High-level approach (sketch):
1) Stratified Stage Consolidation (SSC): group consecutive transformer layers into "slabs" that are co-located onto the same GPU when latency/throughput profile indicates benefit. Slabs are dynamic and can be rebalanced at model load or during low-util windows.
   - Heuristic for slab sizing: target slab token compute time ≈ 2-3x the measured inter-GPU collective latency to amortize NCCL overhead. Smaller slabs increase communication frequency; larger slabs reduce parallelism and memory efficiency.
   - Boundary selection considers KV cache locality: if a layer boundary is hotspot for KV lookups, prefer not to cut there.

2) NCCL Probe-and-Fallback (NPF): a light runtime probe runs periodically or on new allocation to measure pairwise effective bandwidth/latency and operation success rate. If probe indicates incidence of degraded links, switch specific collectives to fallback modes per-collective basis rather than global config.
   - Probe method: send small all-reduce of synthetic payload + checksum; track RTT, throughput, and retry rate. Maintain EWMA of metrics per peer pair.
   - Fallback modes (in order of preference):
     a) Hierarchical collective (intra-node reduce + inter-node aggregator): reduces cross-node traffic and isolates congested NICs.
     b) Elastic degree replication: temporarily replicate KV pages across a small set of GPUs (2x) for reads to avoid collectives for hot tokens; applied only for short-lived spikes.
     c) Serialized rendezvous using TCP-only paths (last resort) with careful backoff to avoid amplifying congestion.

3) KV-cache semantics during consolidation and fallback:
   - Hybrid addressing: use (shard_id, local_offset) as canonical address. When slab relocation or fallback replication occurs, we maintain a small version vector per page to ensure reads see consistent content during short asymmetric replication windows.
   - Hot-page promotion: detect hot KV pages (access frequency + cache miss amplification) and proactively replicate them to nearby slab peers when NCCL KPIs degrade. Replication TTL is short (seconds) and bounded by memory reclaim heuristics.
   - Write path: all writes remain serialized through a primary owner for a page; secondary replicas accept stale reads until a background reconverge (write-through) completes. This keeps write complexity low.

Kernel selection and microbatching implications:
- Kernel scheduling should favor longer contiguous matmul kernels when slabs are large (fewer cross-device hops). But this increases memory pressure and may worsen scheduling for mixed-size requests.
- Microbatch size should be selected per-slab: slab-local microbatching uses continuous KV cache retention to avoid repeated remote fetches. For slabs that span more layers (big slabs), reduce microbatching to keep per-step memory bounded.
- Plan for a "kernel hint" API where the scheduler can request: preferred GEMM tiling, fused attention op, and quantization-friendly path. These hints are attached to slab descriptors on allocation time.

Scheduling heuristics (work in progress):
- On request arrival, assign to slab chain that minimizes estimated remaining time = compute_est + comm_est + queue_wait. comm_est uses current EWMA per-edge from NPF.
- If NPF shows degraded pair A↔B, prefer slab layouts that avoid placing their boundary across that link. This is a soft constraint; if impossible, fall back to hierarchical collectives for that boundary.

Failure modes and safety:
- Probe false positives: short-lived network blips could flip fallback mode unnecessarily. Mitigation: require 2 consecutive probe windows or high error rate before switching fallback. Use decaying backoff to avoid oscillation.
- Memory blowout from opportunistic replication: cap total replicated bytes per node and enforce eviction.
- Consistency hazards: ensure RPC path for cache writes is strongly ordered with a monotonic page version id. Clients reading during transitional periods should be served from the primary or explicit replica list.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- What is an acceptable TTL for hot-page replication? 1s, 5s, 30s? Tradeoffs between memory cost and hit-rate improvements.
- Can we leverage L2/NIC hardware topologies to prefer hierarchical aggregators? Need topology discovery integration with cluster manager.
- How to expose slab boundaries and migration events to the Rollouts/Console so SREs can trace degradations? (Proposal: emit slab allocation telemetry with tags for fallback activation.)

Measurement plan (quick experiments):
1) Controlled NCCL impairment test in CI: introduce packet drop on selected node/port, run representative chat workloads and measure P50/P95/P99 latency and error rates under baseline, SSC-only, and SSC+NPF.
2) Hot KV emulation: artificially generate hot-key access patterns and measure microbatch QPS and memory replication overhead at TTL=1s/5s/30s.
3) Kernel profiling: compare fused attention vs unfused when slabs of size 2/4/8 layers are colocated; capture GPU occupancy and kernel latency distributions.
